level1.text: A $40\,\text{g}$ neodymium magnet falls in a vertical copper tube at a steady speed. How large is the braking force exerted on the magnet by the eddy currents?

A light copper ring hangs from a thread. The south pole of a bar magnet is pushed quickly towards the ring. Which pole appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet, and does the ring repel or attract the magnet?
level1.answer: A south pole appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet, and the ring repels the magnet.

level1.text: An eddy-current brake slows a $450\,\text{kg}$ roller-coaster car on a horizontal track from a speed of $22\,\text{m/s}$ to a speed of $6.0\,\text{m/s}$. Other resistances are ignored. How much energy is converted into internal energy of the copper plates of the brake? Give your answer in kilojoules.
A $25\,\text{g}$ magnet falls in a vertical aluminium tube at a steady speed of $0.30\,\text{m/s}$. At what rate does the internal energy of the tube increase? Give your answer in milliwatts.

Under the glass surface of an induction hob there is a coil carrying a rapidly alternating current. A steel pan on the hob heats up quickly, but the glass surface next to the pan stays cool. Why does the pan heat up but the glass does not?
level1.answer: The alternating magnetic field of the coil induces eddy currents in the electrically conducting base of the pan, and they heat it; glass does not conduct electricity, so no currents appear in it.

level1.text: The north pole of a bar magnet is quickly pulled away from a copper ring. What happens in the ring?
level1.answer: The flux decreases, so the field of the induced current keeps the flux unchanged and the ring attracts the magnet.

choices.text: The flux decreases, so the field of the induced current opposes the field of the magnet and the ring repels the magnet.
choices.feedback: Lenz’s law does not oppose the field but the change in flux. When the flux decreases, the field of the induced current tries to keep it unchanged, that is, it points in the same direction as the field of the magnet. A repelling ring would belong to a situation in which the magnet approaches.

choices.text: The flux increases, so the field of the induced current reduces the flux and the ring repels the magnet.
choices.feedback: When the magnet moves away, the flux through the ring decreases rather than increases. The flux increases only when the magnet approaches the ring; then the ring really does repel the magnet.

choices.text: The flux decreases, so the field of the induced current keeps the flux unchanged and the ring attracts the magnet.
choices.feedback: Correct: the decrease in flux is opposed, so the field of the induced current at the centre of the ring points in the same direction as the field of the magnet. A south pole appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet; it attracts the north pole and opposes the magnet moving away.

choices.text: No current flows in the ring, because copper is not ferromagnetic and so the ring does not interact with the magnet.
choices.feedback: Induction does not require a ferromagnetic material, only an electrically conducting closed loop and a changing flux. Copper conducts electricity well, so when the flux changes an induced current appears in the ring.

level1.text: A neodymium magnet is dropped vertically first in an aluminium tube and then in a similar plastic tube. The magnet falls clearly more slowly in the aluminium tube than in the plastic tube. What explains the difference?
level1.answer: The falling magnet induces eddy currents in the aluminium, and they oppose the motion, but no currents appear in the plastic.

choices.text: Aluminium is ferromagnetic and attracts the magnet, and this attraction slows the fall.
choices.feedback: Aluminium is not a ferromagnetic material, and a stationary magnet does not stick to it. The braking arises only from the motion, because a moving magnet changes the flux and induces eddy currents.

choices.text: Plastic is lighter than aluminium, so gravity pulls the magnet harder in the plastic tube.
choices.feedback: The gravitational force on the magnet depends on the mass of the magnet, not on the material of the tube. The difference arises because braking eddy currents appear only in the electrically conducting tube.

choices.text: The inner surface of the aluminium tube is rougher than that of plastic, so friction slows the magnet more in the aluminium tube.
choices.feedback: Friction does not depend on whether the material of the tube conducts electricity. Eddy-current braking works without contact, and a similar plastic tube is just as smooth as an aluminium one, but the magnet falls freely in it.

choices.text: The falling magnet induces eddy currents in the aluminium, and they oppose the motion, but no currents appear in the plastic.
choices.feedback: Correct: the motion of the magnet changes the flux through the tube, and eddy currents appear in the electrically conducting aluminium. By Lenz’s law they oppose the motion. Plastic is an insulator, so no current flows in it and no braking occurs.

level1.text: A coil has $120$ turns. When a magnet is pushed into the coil, the magnetic flux through one turn increases steadily by $2.5\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.050\,\text{s}$. How large is the induced voltage in the coil?

level2.text: A magnet of mass $20\,\text{g}$ is dropped into a vertical copper tube $1.50\,\text{m}$ long. It emerges from the lower end of the tube after $10\,\text{s}$ and falls at a steady speed for almost the whole distance. At what rate does the internal energy of the tube increase during the fall? Give your answer in milliwatts.

A closed coil has $200$ turns and a resistance of $15\,\Omega$. When a magnet is pushed into the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil increases steadily from zero to $3.0\,\text{mWb}$ in $0.20\,\text{s}$. How large is the induced current in the coil?

A $20\,\text{g}$ magnet falling in a copper tube experiences a braking force from eddy currents that is proportional to the speed of the magnet: $F_\text{j} = k v$, where $k = 1.3\,\tfrac{\text{N}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{m}}$. What final speed does the magnet settle at?

The eddy-current brake of a train exerts a braking force of $60\,\text{kN}$ on the train when the speed of the train is $250\,\text{km/h}$. At what rate does the brake convert the kinetic energy of the train into internal energy of the brake and the rail at this moment? Give your answer in megawatts.

A student drops a $20\,\text{g}$ neodymium magnet into two vertical copper tubes, each $1.00\,\text{m}$ long, with different wall thicknesses. The magnet falls almost the whole distance at a steady speed. The table gives the falling times of five drops (example data).

a) Calculate the mean falling time $t_{\text{avg}}$ for the thick-walled tube and the average speed of the magnet.

b) Calculate the power at which the internal energy of the thick-walled tube increases during the fall. Give your answer in milliwatts.

c) In which tube do the eddy currents brake the magnet more strongly at the same speed? Justify your answer using the measurements and the condition of steady speed.

The result of part b) goes in the answer box.

level2.text:
A student writes in an exam:

“A north pole of a bar magnet approaches a copper ring, and the magnetic flux through the ring increases. The induced current tries to increase this change in flux, so a south pole appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet. The ring attracts the magnet, and the magnet accelerates towards the ring.”

a) What is the error in the reasoning, and which pole really appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet?

b) Why would the student’s rule violate conservation of energy?
level2.answer: The field of the induced current does not increase the change in flux but opposes it: a north pole appears on the side of the ring facing the magnet, and the ring repels the magnet. With the student’s rule the magnet would accelerate by itself and gain kinetic energy without any source of energy.

level2.text:
A student studies a coil with $300$ turns. He pushes a bar magnet into the coil each time the same distance but at different speeds, so the magnetic flux through one turn increases from zero always to the same value $\Delta\Phi$, but in a different time $\Delta t$.

A voltmeter shows the average induced voltage $e$ during the push. The table gives the results of four pushes (example data).

a) For each push calculate the product $e \cdot \Delta t$ and the mean of the products.

b) Use the mean to determine the change in magnetic flux $\Delta\Phi$ in milliwebers.

c) How does the almost equal value of the products show that the induced voltage is inversely proportional to the time $\Delta t$?

The result of part b) goes in the answer box.

data.caption: Induced voltage at different pushing speeds (example data)

level3.text: In a physics lesson a $20\,\text{g}$ magnet is dropped $50$ times in a row through a vertical copper tube $1.00\,\text{m}$ long. Each time it emerges from the lower end at a speed of $0.15\,\text{m/s}$. The mass of the tube is $0.35\,\text{kg}$, and the specific heat capacity of copper is $385\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$. By how much does the temperature of the tube rise if no heat is transferred to the surroundings?

A pendulum made of an aluminium plate swings between the poles of a strong horseshoe magnet. An intact plate stops after only a few swings. When deep slits are sawn into a plate of the same size so that it is comb-shaped, the plate swings between the poles for a long time. Explain the difference.
level3.answer: Large eddy currents appear in the intact plate between the poles; by Lenz's law they brake the motion and convert the mechanical energy of the pendulum into internal energy. The slits cut the current loops, so in the comb-shaped plate the currents and the braking remain small.

level3.text: Two horizontal metal rails are $0.40\,\text{m}$ apart, and their ends are joined by a resistor with a resistance of $0.20\,\Omega$. In the region of the rails there is a vertical magnetic field with a magnetic flux density of $0.50\,\text{T}$. A metal rod lying across the rails moves along them at a speed of $3.0\,\text{m/s}$. The resistance of the rails and the rod is ignored. How large is the braking force that the magnetic field exerts on the rod?

In a physics experiment a $50\,\text{g}$ neodymium magnet is dropped vertically in a thick-walled copper tube, and its speed is measured from a video at different moments (example data).

The braking force of the eddy currents is assumed to be proportional to the speed, $F_\text{j} = k v$. Air resistance and friction are ignored.

a) What is the terminal speed $v_\text{t}$ of the magnet? Use the mean of the last three measurements.

b) How large is the braking force at the terminal speed, and what is the coefficient $k$? Justify why the force is exactly this size then.

c) How large is the acceleration of the magnet at the moment $t = 0.10\,\text{s}$? Draw the $(t, v)$ graph and check the result with the slope between the moments $0.05\,\text{s}$ and $0.15\,\text{s}$.

d) At what power does the internal energy of the tube increase at the terminal speed, and into what does the energy of the magnet turn then?

The acceleration of part c) goes in the answer box.

level3.text:
The alternating magnetic field in the iron core of a transformer induces eddy currents, and they heat the core.

In an experiment the power $P$ of the eddy-current losses was measured for an iron core of the same size when the core was assembled from insulated sheets of different thicknesses. The volume of the core and the alternating magnetic field through it were the same every time, and the sheets were thin compared with the depth to which the field penetrates the iron (example data).

a) Calculate the ratio $P : d^2$ for each measurement. What do the results tell about how the power $P$ depends on the thickness $d$ of the sheet?

b) Calculate the mean $k$ of the ratios.

c) Predict the power of the eddy-current losses when the core consists of sheets $0.35\,\text{mm}$ thick. Give your answer in watts.

d) Use Lenz’s law and eddy currents to justify why thin sheets reduce the loss. How many times greater would the loss be with $1.0\,\text{mm}$ sheets than with $0.35\,\text{mm}$ sheets?

The power of part c) goes in the answer box.

data.caption: Eddy-current losses as a function of the thickness of the sheets (example data)
